imr.title: Individuals and moving range chart
imr.summary: Monitor one numerical measurement at each sampling occasion.
imr.why: An X-mR chart tracks individual measurements and their successive differences when there are no rational subgroups.

setup.title: Assign the measurements
setup.text: Place the numerical column in Measurement. Place the sequence or time label in Timestamp (optional). Keep the rows in their actual collection order.

setup.title: Select the chart
setup.text: Select X-mR chart. A moving range length of 2 uses successive pairs.

setup.title: Check stability and dependence
setup.text: Inspect both charts and select Autocorrelation. Investigate signals before treating the observed period as stable; this interface estimates its center and limits from the plotted data.

columns.name: sequence
columns.description: Ordered sampling occasion; rows remain in time order.

columns.name: fill_ml
columns.description: One fill-volume measurement per occasion, in mL.

checks: Measurements must represent comparable conditions. Use Stage for documented changes when separate phases are appropriate; each stage is estimated separately, rather than monitored against a frozen earlier baseline.
Strong serial dependence, severe skewness, or changing measurement resolution can make conventional limits misleading.
Control limits describe process behaviour. They are different from customer specification limits.
A chart with no signal does not establish that the process meets specifications.
report: Report the period used to estimate the limits, measurement units, chart rules, and how control limits were obtained.
Describe signals and their investigation; absence of a signal is not proof of permanent stability.

example.title: One bottle every few minutes
example.story: A filling line records one bottle volume at each sampling occasion. Check whether its behaviour changes over time.
instructions: Assign fill_ml to Measurement and sequence to Timestamp (optional).
Inspect the individuals chart together with the moving range chart.

related.label: Compare a stable process with specifications

xbar_r.title: X-bar and R charts
xbar_r.summary: Monitor subgroup averages and within-subgroup ranges.
xbar_r.why: You measure several units under similar conditions at each occasion. The range chart is a conventional choice for small subgroups, commonly 2–9 units.

setup.title: Use the subgroup structure
setup.text: Select Single column. Put the numerical values in Measurement and the subgroup identifier in Subgroups.

setup.title: Define the grouping
setup.text: Select Through grouping variable. Use unique subgroup labels and Same subgroup value, or retain consecutive groups with Subgroup value change.

setup.title: Choose the charts
setup.text: Under Control charts select X-bar & R. Use actual sizes if subgroup sizes differ.

setup.title: Read variation first
setup.text: Inspect the R chart before interpreting the X-bar chart. Investigate special causes and keep an audit trail of any exclusions.

columns.name: subgroup
columns.description: Sampling occasion; the example has five measurements per subgroup.

columns.name: diameter_mm
columns.description: Measured shaft diameter in mm.

checks: Form rational subgroups: units measured close together under comparable conditions.
Do not make arbitrary groups from a time series simply to obtain a smaller standard error.
Independence within and between subgroups matters; substantial dependence needs a different monitoring model.
Control limits are not acceptance or specification limits.
report: Describe subgroup size, sampling interval, chart rules, and the baseline period.
Report mean and variation signals separately, with their process explanations.

example.title: Five shafts per sample
example.story: Five successive shafts are measured at each scheduled sample. The charts separate changes in average diameter from changes in short-term spread.
instructions: Assign diameter_mm to Measurement and subgroup to Subgroups.
Choose Through grouping variable and X-bar & R.

xbar_s.title: X-bar and s charts
xbar_s.summary: Monitor subgroup averages and standard deviations.
xbar_s.why: Each occasion has a rational subgroup of numerical observations. Standard deviations use more information than ranges and are usually preferred for larger subgroups, commonly 10 or more.

setup.title: Assign long-format data
setup.text: Select Single column. Assign the outcome to Measurement and the sample identifier to Subgroups.

setup.title: Specify the subgroups
setup.text: Choose Through grouping variable. With unique labels, Same subgroup value combines the rows from each sampling occasion.

setup.title: Select X-bar & s
setup.text: Under Control charts select X-bar & s. Retain Use actual sizes when sample sizes differ.

setup.title: Review both charts
setup.text: Inspect the s chart for unstable spread before interpreting subgroup averages.

columns.name: subgroup
columns.description: Sampling occasion; the example has ten measurements per subgroup.

columns.name: diameter_mm
columns.description: One measured shaft diameter per row, in mm.

checks: Subgroups should capture short-term common-cause variation, with comparable operating conditions inside each subgroup.
The size threshold is a practical convention, not a mathematical boundary between valid and invalid charts.
Highly skewed data, extreme observations, or dependence warrant closer distributional and process checks.
When the process changes, consider documented phases instead of pooling incompatible operating periods.
report: Report subgroup construction, sample sizes, baseline, and the chart rules used.
Describe signals in the average and dispersion charts and any investigated causes.

example.title: Ten shafts per sample
example.story: The same process is sampled in groups of ten, making the standard deviation a useful measure of within-sample spread.
instructions: Assign diameter_mm to Measurement and subgroup to Subgroups.
Choose Through grouping variable and X-bar & s.

p_chart.title: p chart
p_chart.summary: Monitor the fraction of units classified as nonconforming.
p_chart.why: Each inspected unit has one binary classification. A p chart accommodates differing numbers inspected at successive occasions.

setup.title: Supply counts and denominators
setup.text: Assign the count of nonconforming units to Defectives/Defects and the number inspected to Total. Assign batch to Timestamp (optional).

setup.title: Select the binomial chart
setup.text: Under Charts for Attributes select Defectives, then p chart.

setup.title: Review the limits
setup.text: With varying denominators, limits may vary by occasion. The reviewed interface estimates the reference fraction from the plotted data, rather than a fixed earlier baseline. Investigate signals using production and inspection records.

columns.name: batch
columns.description: Inspection occasion in chronological order.

columns.name: rejected
columns.description: Integer count of nonconforming units.

columns.name: inspected
columns.description: Positive integer count of all inspected units.

checks: Count each unit once, even if it has several defects. The rejected count cannot exceed the inspected count.
The binomial model assumes comparable classification probabilities within each sample and approximately independent units.
Changing product mix, clustering, or inspection practice can create extra variation. Investigate these before considering the available Laney p-prime option.
Very rare outcomes and small denominators may need more specialised chart design.
report: Report the overall fraction, sample denominators, baseline, and any signal investigation.
State that limits describe expected process variation, not an allowable rejection threshold.

example.title: Reject fraction across batches
example.story: Inspect different numbers of units in each batch and ask whether the rejection fraction has changed.
instructions: Assign rejected to Defectives/Defects and inspected to Total.
Select Defectives and p chart; keep batch order.

related.label: Several defects can occur on one unit

np_chart.title: np chart
np_chart.summary: Monitor the number of nonconforming units in equally sized samples.
np_chart.why: Each unit is classified once and the number inspected is constant. The chart displays counts in the original inspection units.

setup.title: Assign inspection counts
setup.text: Put rejected in Defectives/Defects, inspected in Total, and batch in Timestamp (optional).

setup.title: Select the count chart
setup.text: Choose Defectives, then np chart.

setup.title: Review time-ordered behaviour
setup.text: Inspect the count series and its control limits, estimated from the plotted data rather than a fixed earlier baseline. Link signals to operational records and inspection changes.

columns.name: batch
columns.description: Inspection occasion in actual collection order.

columns.name: rejected
columns.description: Number of nonconforming units in the sample.

columns.name: inspected
columns.description: The same positive sample size for every row.

checks: The denominator must be constant; use a p chart when the number inspected varies.
A unit is counted only once, regardless of how many defects it contains.
Binomial assumptions can fail with clustering, changing mix, or inconsistent inspection.
A low rejection count does not by itself show that a customer acceptance criterion has been met.
report: Report the fixed sample size, average count, monitoring rules, and baseline period.
Describe any signals and follow-up investigation without treating every signal as a confirmed cause.

example.title: Inspect 100 units per batch
example.story: An inspector checks exactly 100 units in each batch and records how many fail the specified inspection.
instructions: Assign rejected to Defectives/Defects and inspected to Total.
Select Defectives and np chart.

related.label: Count defects rather than defective units

c_chart.title: c chart
c_chart.summary: Monitor defect counts with a constant inspection opportunity.
c_chart.why: You count occurrences, and one unit can contain more than one defect. The inspected area, quantity, or exposure stays constant.

setup.title: Assign defect counts
setup.text: Put the defect count in Defectives/Defects. Put the constant number of inspected units in Total and batch in Timestamp (optional).

setup.title: Choose the Poisson count chart
setup.text: Start fresh with the inactive Defectives selection at np, then choose Defects and c chart.

setup.title: Check the operational context
setup.text: The reviewed interface estimates the reference count from the plotted data, rather than a fixed earlier baseline. Interpret changes alongside inspection coverage, product mix, and changes in how defects are detected.

setup.title: Colleague preview — 7 November 2026
setup.text: Preview workaround: start a fresh analysis, keep the inactive Defectives selection at np, then choose Defects → c. This avoids the audited count-versus-exposure guard. All 30 original counts remain. Center 8.2, LCL 0, UCL 16.790693; batch 21 exceeds its upper limit.

columns.name: batch
columns.description: Inspection occasion in chronological order.

columns.name: defects
columns.description: Non-negative integer count; multiple defects on one unit are allowed.

columns.name: units_inspected
columns.description: Constant inspection exposure; ten comparable units per example sample.

checks: Inspection opportunities must be comparable. Equal unit counts are insufficient if unit size or inspection coverage changes.
A c chart uses Poisson variation; clusters of defects or different underlying rates may violate this model.
Use a u chart for variable inspection exposure.
These are defect counts, not counts of units with at least one defect.

Preview workaround: start a fresh analysis, keep the inactive Defectives selection at np, then choose Defects → c. This avoids the audited count-versus-exposure guard. All 30 original counts remain. Center 8.2, LCL 0, UCL 16.790693; batch 21 exceeds its upper limit.
report: Report the count per fixed inspection sample and define the sample size or area.
Describe signals, the baseline, and any evidence of clustering or overdispersion.

example.title: Surface flaws in ten panels
example.story: Each inspection sample contains ten equally sized panels. Count every surface flaw, including multiple flaws on a panel.
instructions: Assign defects to Defectives/Defects and units_inspected to Total.
Start fresh with the inactive Defectives selection at np, then choose Defects and c chart.

related.label: Each unit is only pass or fail

u_chart.title: u chart
u_chart.summary: Monitor defects per unit when inspection exposure varies.
u_chart.why: One unit can have multiple defects and the inspected quantity changes. A u chart divides counts by their exposure and adjusts limits accordingly.

setup.title: Define a consistent exposure unit
setup.text: Use the number of comparable units, area, or other justified inspection exposure as the denominator.

setup.title: Assign the variables
setup.text: Assign defects to Defectives/Defects, exposure_half_panel_units to Total, and batch to Timestamp.

setup.title: Select the rate chart
setup.text: Choose Defects, then u chart. Review the varying control limits together with the denominators; the reference rate is estimated from the plotted data rather than a fixed earlier baseline.

setup.title: Colleague preview — 7 November 2026
setup.text: Ordinary u preview: exposure_half_panel_units = 2 × units_inspected. One exposure unit is half a panel’s area, not an additional inspected panel. All 30 counts remain; rates and limits halve. Center .383333 defects per half-panel area. The current axis may say Proportion and the rule table misses batch 27. Compare each point with its own limits: batch 27 has .7 against UCL .677017 and is the sole beyond-limit point.

columns.name: batch
columns.description: Inspection occasion in chronological order.

columns.name: defects
columns.description: Non-negative integer count of defect occurrences.

columns.name: units_inspected
columns.description: Positive inspection exposure in a consistent unit.

columns.name: exposure_half_panel_units
columns.description: Twice units_inspected, expressed as half-panel area; not extra inspected panels.

checks: A Poisson rate model requires comparable opportunity per exposure unit and approximately independent occurrences.
Defect counts can exceed the number of units; a u value is a rate, not a probability.
Investigate clustering, mix changes, and overdispersion before considering the available Laney u-prime chart.
A denominator of zero is invalid and should be resolved before analysis.

Ordinary u preview: exposure_half_panel_units = 2 × units_inspected. One exposure unit is half a panel’s area, not an additional inspected panel. All 30 counts remain; rates and limits halve. Center .383333 defects per half-panel area. The current axis may say Proportion and the rule table misses batch 27. Compare each point with its own limits: batch 27 has .7 against UCL .677017 and is the sole beyond-limit point.
report: Report the rate with its exposure unit, baseline, and sample denominators.
Describe signals and assess whether changing inspection opportunity explains them.

example.title: Flaws per half-panel area — ordinary u preview
example.story: Synthetic teaching data: all original varying-exposure observations and counts, with an equivalent half-panel area denominator.
instructions: Assign defects to Defectives/Defects, exposure_half_panel_units to Total, and batch to Timestamp.
Choose ordinary Defects → u, not Laney. Interpret rates per half-panel area and independently compare each point with its own limits.

ewma.title: Exponentially weighted moving average chart
ewma.summary: Look for small, sustained changes in a numerical process.
ewma.why: An EWMA combines current and previous measurements, giving more weight to recent observations. It can reveal persistent changes that individual-point charts may miss.

setup.title: Assign the observations
setup.text: Select Single column. Assign the numerical outcome to Measurement and the sequence label to Timestamp (optional).

setup.title: Specify the sampling design
setup.text: Select No subgroups (n = 1) for individual observations. For rational subgroups, supply their actual grouping structure.

setup.title: Select EWMA
setup.text: Select Exponentially weighted moving average chart, lambda .5, three-sigma limits and moving-range SD with length 2.

setup.title: Understand the reference used
setup.text: Use a justified estimate of in-control SD, or enter an independently established historical SD. The reviewed implementation still uses the current stage’s mean for the center and initial EWMA value; historical SD does not fix a historical mean.

setup.title: Colleague preview — 7 November 2026
setup.text: Retrospective faster-weighting preview: all 60 original observations, no subgroups, moving-range SD of length 2, lambda .5 and three-sigma limits. Center 501.8645 mL; 19 of 60 points exceed their limits and have red markers. No pooled SD is used. Historical SD would not freeze the mean or make this prospective monitoring.

columns.name: sequence
columns.description: Sampling occasion, ordered in time.

columns.name: fill_ml
columns.description: One numerical fill-volume measurement per occasion.

checks: Small lambda values retain a longer memory; sensitivity and false-alarm behaviour depend jointly on lambda and limit settings.
Serial dependence can create spurious signals; an EWMA does not automatically correct autocorrelation.

This implementation supports retrospective assessment, not monitoring against a frozen historical mean. Stage estimates separate means; adding later observations can change earlier EWMA values. Do not treat a period containing a known change as an established in-control baseline.
Use a standard individuals or subgroup chart to understand gross instability and variation first.

Retrospective faster-weighting preview: all 60 original observations, no subgroups, moving-range SD of length 2, lambda .5 and three-sigma limits. Center 501.8645 mL; 19 of 60 points exceed their limits and have red markers. No pooled SD is used. Historical SD would not freeze the mean or make this prospective monitoring.
report: Report lambda, limit settings, the period used to estimate the center, the SD source and value, and the sampling interval.
State the timing and persistence of any signals and the operational follow-up.

example.title: Gradual change in filling
example.story: Use the fill-volume series to inspect a possible sustained small shift retrospectively. The center is estimated from the plotted period; this example is not a calibrated prospective alarm design.
instructions: Assign fill_ml and sequence; retain all 60 observations with No subgroups (n=1).
Select Exponentially weighted moving average chart, lambda .5, three-sigma limits and moving-range SD with length 2.
Interpret this as retrospective faster weighting; verify center 501.8645 mL and 19 beyond-limit points.

cusum.title: Cumulative sum chart
cusum.summary: Detect persistent departures from a specified process target.
cusum.why: A CUSUM accumulates evidence of a sustained shift. Its target, shift setting, and limits should reflect the change that matters in the process.

setup.title: Assign time-ordered measurements
setup.text: Select Single column and assign the outcome to Measurement. Set No subgroups (n = 1) for one observation per occasion.

setup.title: Choose CUSUM and enter the target
setup.text: Select Cumulative sum chart. Enter Target in the outcome units; the default zero is not the correct target for every process.

setup.title: Specify sensitivity and variation
setup.text: Review Shift size, Number of std. dev. for control limits, and Std. dev. source. Use a stable baseline or justified historical variation.

setup.title: Investigate sustained signals
setup.text: Review the accumulation against operational changes. Preserve the baseline and chosen settings in the report.

columns.name: sequence
columns.description: Sampling occasion in actual time order.

columns.name: fill_ml
columns.description: Numerical fill volume; the example target is 500 mL.

checks: The target and sensitivity settings must be chosen for the operational question, not tuned until a preferred signal appears.
Conventional CUSUM calculations assume suitable independence and a stable in-control distribution.
The shift and limit settings jointly affect detection delay and false alarms.
A CUSUM signal is a reason to investigate, not proof that a particular process cause is responsible.
report: Report the target, shift and limit settings, variation estimate, baseline period, and sampling frequency.
Explain the process interpretation of sustained upward or downward accumulation.

example.title: Filling around a 500 mL target
example.story: A filling line aims for 500 mL. Ask whether deviations accumulate persistently on either side of the target.
instructions: Select Cumulative sum chart and enter Target = 500.
Document the displayed shift and limit settings; use the example to learn the workflow.

cap_normal.title: Normal process capability study
cap_normal.summary: Compare a stable numerical process with engineering specifications.
cap_normal.why: A normal model is plausible, specifications are defined independently of the data, and the sampling design supports a meaningful estimate of process variation.

setup.title: Assign data and subgrouping
setup.text: Select Single column and assign the outcome to Measurement. Set Subgroup size = 1 for individual time-ordered observations; otherwise enter the real subgroup structure.

setup.title: Specify the model and requirements
setup.text: Under Process capability options choose Normal distribution. Enter the applicable Lower specification limit, Upper specification limit, and optional Target value.

setup.title: Request the relevant output
setup.text: Select Process capability tables and Confidence intervals. Review the Process capability plot and Probability table and plot.

setup.title: Check stability before the indices
setup.text: Review Stability of the process, including its variation chart. Treat capability from an unstable or mixed process as an inadequate forecast of future production.

columns.name: sequence
columns.description: Collection order; retain chronological row order.

columns.name: fill_ml
columns.description: Measured fill volume in mL.

checks: Specification limits come from requirements; control limits are estimated from process behaviour.
Check stability, measurement adequacy, representativeness, and the distribution, especially the tails.
Do not accept normality merely because a normality test is nonsignificant.
For a single specification limit, use the corresponding one-sided index; a two-sided Cp needs both limits.
report: Report the specifications, data period, subgroup structure, distribution, and variation estimator.
Distinguish Cp/Cpk based on within-process variation from Pp/Ppk based on overall variation; include uncertainty.
Compare estimates with the agreed customer requirement, and interpret centring separately from spread.

example.title: A centred process with too much variation
example.story: A filling process targets 500 mL with limits of 490 and 510 mL. Explore why good centring alone cannot ensure capability.
instructions: Set Subgroup size = 1, LSL = 490, USL = 510, Target = 500.
Review stability and the probability plot before interpreting capability.

cap_nonnormal.title: Non-normal process capability study
cap_nonnormal.summary: Assess specification performance using a justified non-normal distribution.
cap_nonnormal.why: The outcome is numerical and stable, but its shape is not adequately represented by a normal distribution. Model choice should reflect the process and tail behaviour.

setup.title: Assign measurements and grouping
setup.text: Use Single column and Measurement. Set Subgroup size = 1 for individual observations, or enter the real rational subgroups.

setup.title: Choose a distribution
setup.text: Under Process capability options select Non-normal distribution and Specify a distribution. Options include Log-normal, Weibull, Gamma, Exponential, Logistic, and Log-logistic.

setup.title: Enter specifications and inspect fit
setup.text: Enter only the applicable specification limits. Inspect the histogram, Probability table and plot, and process stability.

setup.title: Choose the index convention
setup.text: Review Non-normal capability statistics: Percentile or Non-conformance. Document the chosen convention and fitted distribution.

columns.name: sequence
columns.description: Collection order for the uncensored process measurements.

columns.name: cycle_seconds
columns.description: Positive, fully observed cycle duration in seconds.

checks: Choose a plausible model; searching for the largest capability index is not model validation.
Check the domain and tails. For example, standard log-normal and Weibull models require positive measurements.
Separate mixtures or unstable operating regimes before fitting a single capability distribution.
Censored lifetimes require a survival-analysis workflow; do not treat unfinished runs as observed failure times.
Normal-model confidence intervals are not offered for this non-normal option in the verified baseline.
report: Report the model, fitting choices, specification limits, index convention, and data period.
Discuss sensitivity of tail performance to plausible distributions and the amount of tail data available.

example.title: Right-skewed cycle times
example.story: Cycle times are positive and right-skewed. The operational requirement is completion within 60 seconds.
instructions: Select Log-normal as an illustrative candidate and enter only USL = 60.
Inspect the probability plot before interpreting estimated nonconformance.

gage_crossed.title: Crossed gauge repeatability and reproducibility
gage_crossed.summary: Separate measurement repeatability, operator differences, and part variation.
gage_crossed.why: Every operator measures the same set of parts repeatedly. This crossed design allows operator-by-part behaviour to be examined.

setup.title: Set up the study data
setup.text: Use Single column. Assign the numerical value to Measurement, operator identifier to Operator, and part identifier to Part.

setup.title: Specify the comparison basis
setup.text: Review Std. dev. source. Enter Tolerance width when comparison with engineering tolerance is needed; this is USL minus LSL.

setup.title: Inspect components and plots
setup.text: Request the r&R ANOVA table, variation components, and relevant range and operator-by-part plots.

setup.title: Review modelling choices
setup.text: Document the operator model, study-variation multiplier, and interaction-removal setting. Type 3 study (automatic equipment) is available when there is no operator factor.

columns.name: part
columns.description: The same physical parts are measured by each operator.

columns.name: operator
columns.description: Operator identifier.

columns.name: trial
columns.description: Repeat number; retain for study records.

columns.name: diameter_mm
columns.description: Repeated diameter measurement in mm.

checks: Use representative parts spanning the operating range; randomise measurement order and conceal previous readings.
Include genuine repeated measurements for every operator–part combination.
Percent contribution uses variances; percent study variation uses standard deviations. Their numerical thresholds differ.
Agreement of measurements does not establish calibration accuracy without reference values.
report: Report repeatability, reproducibility, and total gauge variation with their comparison basis.
Describe the design, tolerance, operator-by-part patterns, and agreed acceptance criteria.

example.title: Three operators, ten parts, two repeats
example.story: Each operator measures each of ten shafts twice. Explore whether variation is mainly repeatability, operator differences, or their interaction.
instructions: Assign diameter_mm to Measurement, operator to Operator, and part to Part.
Keep trial for auditability; it is not a separate required analysis role.

related.label: Operators cannot measure the same parts

gage_nested.title: Nested gauge r&R for non-replicable measurements
gage_nested.summary: Assess measurement variation when each operator receives different parts or homogeneous specimen groups.
gage_nested.why: Parts are nested within operators. For destructive testing, replicate specimens must plausibly represent the same homogeneous material group.

setup.title: Confirm the design
setup.text: Each part/group identifier belongs to one operator. Include balanced replicate measurements or equivalent homogeneous specimens within each operator–part group.

setup.title: Assign the columns
setup.text: Select Single column. Put strength_mpa in Measurements, operator in Operators, and part in Parts.

setup.title: Set the comparison basis
setup.text: Review Std. dev. source and optionally enter Tolerance width. Request the r&R ANOVA table and Graph variation components.

setup.title: Examine the nested components
setup.text: Read the nested ANOVA and gauge evaluation alongside the measurements-by-part and operator plots.

setup.title: Colleague preview — 7 November 2026
setup.text: This exact balanced, globally unique-part example gives repeatability variance .5684717, operator 0 and part 17.2412365. The module has an operator denominator defect; both correct and defective estimates truncate to zero here. Zero estimated operator variance does not establish operator equivalence. Do not generalize this preview to positive operator components or other designs.

columns.name: operator
columns.description: Operator assigned to a distinct set of part groups.

columns.name: part
columns.description: Unique part/group identifier nested within one operator.

columns.name: replicate
columns.description: Repeat or homogeneous specimen within a part group.

columns.name: strength_mpa
columns.description: Observed destructive-test strength in MPa.

checks: A destructive test does not automatically justify this design: the assumed within-group specimen homogeneity must be defensible.
One observation per operator–part group cannot identify a separate repeatability component.
Use the same number of replicates per part group and the same number of part groups per operator for this baseline implementation.
Residual specimen differences can be confounded with repeatability; document that practical limitation.

This exact balanced, globally unique-part example gives repeatability variance .5684717, operator 0 and part 17.2412365. The module has an operator denominator defect; both correct and defective estimates truncate to zero here. Zero estimated operator variance does not establish operator equivalence. Do not generalize this preview to positive operator components or other designs.
report: Report the nesting, replicate construction, homogeneity assumption, and variance comparison basis.
Interpret operator and repeatability components in light of the available replication and specimen variation.

example.title: Destructive strength testing
example.story: Three operators test their own sets of material groups. Two nominally homogeneous specimens from each group supply the within-group replication.
instructions: Assign strength_mpa to Measurements, operator to Operators, and part to Parts.
Keep part IDs unique across operators; explain why paired specimens are comparable.

related.label: All operators can remeasure the same parts

gage_type1.title: Type 1 instrument capability study
gage_type1.summary: Evaluate repeatability and bias at one known reference value.
gage_type1.why: One instrument repeatedly measures a reference artefact. The reference value and tolerance width let you assess instrument variation and bias at that point.

setup.title: Assign repeated measurements
setup.text: Put the measurement column in Measurement. Preserve collection order for the run chart.

setup.title: Enter calibration information
setup.text: Set Reference/master value and Tolerance range. Review Percent of tolerance for Cg and Number of std. dev. for instrument variation.

setup.title: Review bias and capability
setup.text: Request Bias and instrument capability table and One sample t-test with Confidence interval for bias.

setup.title: Inspect the sequence
setup.text: Use the Run chart and Histogram to identify drift, unusual readings, or inadequate resolution.

columns.name: repeat
columns.description: Sequential measurement number.

columns.name: length_mm
columns.description: Repeated measurement of the same reference artefact in mm.

checks: The reference value should be traceable and sufficiently precise for the intended assessment.
Use a stable instrument and consistent procedure; repeated readings must reflect real measurement repetitions.
A result at one reference value does not establish acceptable bias over the full operating range.
Small statistical bias may be operationally negligible; assess its interval against practical requirements.
report: Report the reference value, tolerance range, Cg/Cgk settings, bias estimate, and bias interval.
Explain whether the instrument meets the agreed requirements at this reference point.

example.title: Repeatedly measuring a 25 mm standard
example.story: Measure a 25.000 mm reference artefact repeatedly to assess short-term precision and bias.
instructions: Set Reference/master value = 25.000 and Tolerance range = 0.100 mm.
Assign length_mm to Measurement and inspect the run chart as well as the capability table.

gage_linearity.title: Type 4 linearity study
gage_linearity.summary: Check whether measurement bias changes across the operating range.
gage_linearity.why: You have several reference parts spanning the measurement range and repeated readings for each. The analysis relates measurement bias to the reference value.

setup.title: Prepare reference measurements
setup.text: Use one row per reading, with a part identifier, its reference value, and the measured value.

setup.title: Assign the analysis roles
setup.text: Put part in Parts, measured_mm in Measurements, and reference_mm in Standard.

setup.title: Inspect bias and linearity
setup.text: Request Linearity table, Bias table, and Linearity and bias graph.

setup.title: Optional process comparison
setup.text: Enter Process variation only when you have a justified value and need the corresponding percent process variation graph.

columns.name: part
columns.description: Reference artefact identifier.

columns.name: reference_mm
columns.description: Known reference value for that part, in mm.

columns.name: measured_mm
columns.description: Observed repeated reading, in mm.

checks: Reference values should span the intended operating range and have appropriate traceability.
Use multiple genuine repeats at each reference; do not substitute repeated copies of the same result.
A nonsignificant slope does not demonstrate negligible bias or adequate precision.
Assess the size and uncertainty of bias throughout the range, including any constant offset.
report: Report reference coverage, repeats per part, the bias estimates, and the linearity result.
Explain whether the observed bias pattern is acceptable across the intended range and whether recalibration is needed.

example.title: Five reference sizes
example.story: An instrument is checked with reference artefacts of several sizes. Repeated measurements reveal whether larger items are increasingly overestimated.
instructions: Assign part to Parts, measured_mm to Measurements, and reference_mm to Standard.
Read the bias table together with the Linearity and bias graph.

attribute_agreement.title: Attributes agreement analysis
attribute_agreement.summary: Assess consistency of categorical inspection decisions.
attribute_agreement.why: Operators repeatedly classify the same parts. With a trusted reference classification you can also assess agreement with the standard.

setup.title: Use repeated categorical ratings
setup.text: Select Single column. Assign rating to Results, operator to Operator, and part to Part.

setup.title: Add the standard if available
setup.text: Assign the trusted reference classification to Standard. Without it, agreement among operators cannot establish accuracy.

setup.title: Choose the binary study
setup.text: Use Kappa study with Positive reference = Pass. In this A/B demonstration request Cohen’s kappa; leave Fleiss’ kappa off.

setup.title: Inspect agreement components
setup.text: Review within-appraiser, between-appraiser, and standard-comparison output. With Pass as Positive reference, the miss rate is the fraction of reference-Fail ratings called Pass; the false-alarm rate is the fraction of reference-Pass ratings called Fail.

setup.title: Colleague preview — 7 November 2026
setup.text: Explicit two-appraiser A/B demonstration: 48 original ratings, all 12 parts and both trials; Positive reference = Pass. Appraiser C is excluded because perfect agreement triggers a confidence-interval failure. The full original 72-rating dataset remains separately available in the example library. For each appraiser, 10/12 parts agree across trials, 22/24 ratings agree with the standard, kappa .828571; missed failures 1/10 and false alarms 1/14.

checks: Use blind, randomised repeats and representative cases, including difficult or borderline examples.
Kappa depends on category prevalence and marginal rating frequencies; inspect raw agreement and error patterns too.
Kendall’s tau is available for ordered ratings, but association is not the same as exact agreement.
This worked path uses binary labels. More complex category structures need the appropriate agreement model and coding.
